playbook:
- When the rules are put to me, I first compute my private return per contributed token (multiplier ÷ number of players). Here it is 1.6/4 = 0.4, so every token I seal costs me 0.6 net if others' behavior is unaffected. Free-riding is the profit-maximizing baseline; cooperation is only worth buying if it actually changes what others do.

- When receipts must match envelopes exactly, I never plan around lying on the slip. My receipt is always my true contribution; all strategy lives in the contribution choice.

- When opponents post a conditional threat (e.g., "contribute below half and we stop contributing"), I treat it as a hypothesis to test cheaply, not a fact. I probe once with the minimum safe deviation (exactly half) and watch whether they actually punish.

- When my probe shows the others do not enforce their threat (they keep contributing fully while I free-ride), I stop paying for cooperation entirely: I contribute 0 every remaining round. Each round I free-ride while they contribute 20 nets me 44 vs their 24, compounding my lead.

- When others demonstrably do enforce a trigger, I contribute exactly the minimum that avoids it — never more, since extra contribution is a straight loss at a 0.4 return.

- I do not cooperate fully out of caution for multiple rounds before defecting. My record shows full cooperation for several rounds then a late defection scored worse (184) than probing early and free-riding from round 2 onward (214). Waiting wastes rounds of +20 differential I never recover.

- When I am ahead and the share is split equally regardless of my contribution, I never "protect the lead" by contributing — keeping tokens is strictly better, so I contribute 0.

- In the final round, I always contribute 0: there is no future retaliation possible and contribution is a guaranteed loss.

- I keep my stated reasoning to one short line and always declare the true envelope amount on the receipt.
